units.name: Foundations of Democracy

concepts.intro: The Framers drew on Enlightenment philosophy to reject monarchy and design a republic that balances majority rule with protection of individual rights.
b: Natural rights (Locke): life, liberty, property/pursuit of happiness exist prior to government; government's job is to secure them
Social contract: legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed, who may alter or abolish it if it fails them
Direct democracy vs. representative democracy (republic): the U.S. is a republic — citizens elect representatives to make laws rather than voting on every law themselves
Participatory democracy emphasizes broad citizen engagement (town halls, referenda); pluralist democracy emphasizes group competition; elite theory holds that a small, wealthy elite dominates policy
Federalist No. 10 (Madison) argues a large republic controls the 'mischiefs of faction' by diluting any single group's power across many competing interests

concepts.intro: America's first national government (1781–1789) was deliberately weak, reflecting fear of tyranny after British rule, but its weaknesses nearly destroyed the young nation.
b: Congress could not levy taxes or regulate interstate/foreign commerce — it could only request money and cooperation from states
No independent executive or national judiciary existed to enforce or interpret laws
Amendment required unanimous consent of all 13 states, making change nearly impossible
Each state had one vote regardless of population, and 9 of 13 states had to agree to pass major legislation
Shays' Rebellion (1786–87), an armed uprising of indebted Massachusetts farmers, exposed the government's inability to maintain order and directly prompted the Constitutional Convention

concepts.intro: Delegates meeting in Philadelphia in 1787 resolved deep disputes between large and small states, and between North and South, through a series of compromises.
b: Virginia Plan: bicameral legislature with representation based on population, favoring large states
New Jersey Plan: unicameral legislature with equal representation per state, favoring small states
Great (Connecticut) Compromise: created a bicameral Congress — the House apportioned by population, the Senate with equal representation (2 per state)
Three-Fifths Compromise: counted enslaved people as three-fifths of a person for both representation and taxation purposes

Compromise on the slave trade delayed a federal ban on importing enslaved persons until 1808; the Electoral College was created as a compromise between direct popular election and congressional selection of the president

concepts.intro: The Constitution divides sovereignty between a national government and the states, a structure designed to prevent any single level from becoming too powerful.
b: Enumerated (expressed) powers belong to the national government (coin money, declare war, regulate interstate commerce)
Reserved powers belong to the states under the Tenth Amendment (police power, education, intrastate commerce)
Concurrent powers are shared by both levels (taxation, building roads, establishing courts)
The Necessary and Proper (Elastic) Clause (Article I, Section 8) lets Congress pass laws needed to execute its enumerated powers — the basis for implied powers

The Supremacy Clause (Article VI) makes federal law supreme over conflicting state law; federalism has shifted over time from dual federalism ('layer cake') toward cooperative federalism ('marble cake') via grants-in-aid, categorical grants, and block grants

concepts.intro: Ratification of the Constitution sparked a fierce national debate over how much power the new central government should hold.
b: Federalists (Hamilton, Madison, Jay) supported a strong national government and defended the Constitution in the Federalist Papers

Federalist No. 10 argues a large, extended republic best controls factions; Federalist No. 51 argues separation of powers and checks and balances ('ambition must be made to counteract ambition') prevent tyranny
Anti-Federalists (e.g., Brutus) feared a strong central government would recreate the tyranny of the British monarchy and threaten state sovereignty and individual liberty
Anti-Federalists demanded a Bill of Rights as the price of ratification, since the original Constitution lacked explicit protections for individual liberties
The compromise: the Constitution was ratified in 1788, and the first ten amendments (Bill of Rights) were added in 1791

concepts.l: Separation of Powers & Checks and Balances
concepts.intro: The Constitution divides national power among three branches, each able to check the others, to prevent tyranny while enabling government to function.
b: Legislative (Article I) makes law, Executive (Article II) enforces law, Judicial (Article III) interprets law

Checks include: presidential veto (Congress can override with 2/3 vote in both chambers), Senate confirmation of appointments and treaties, judicial review (courts can strike down unconstitutional laws)
Impeachment: the House impeaches (majority vote) and the Senate tries and convicts (2/3 vote) — used against presidents, judges, and other officials
Federalist No. 51: structuring government so each branch has the 'constitutional means and personal motives to resist encroachments' of the others
This system trades efficiency for the protection of liberty, often producing gridlock by design

keyFacts: The Constitution can be formally amended only two ways: 2/3 proposal in both houses of Congress (or a national convention called by 2/3 of states) followed by ratification by 3/4 of states — only 27 amendments exist since 1789
Federalist No. 10 and No. 51, written by James Madison, are required foundational documents and appear constantly on the exam
The Tenth Amendment reserves all powers not delegated to the national government, nor prohibited to the states, to the states or the people
Brutus No. 1, an Anti-Federalist paper, argued a republic 'so extensive' as the proposed union could not preserve liberty — the opposite claim from Federalist No. 10
traps: The U.S. is a republic (representative democracy), not a direct democracy — citizens elect representatives rather than voting directly on national laws
Federalism divides power between national and state governments; separation of powers divides power among the three branches of the SAME (national) government — these are often confused
The Great Compromise created a bicameral Congress; it did NOT resolve the slavery question — that required the separate Three-Fifths Compromise
Implied powers come from the Necessary and Proper Clause, not from the Tenth Amendment — the Tenth Amendment is about RESERVED powers to the states

units.name: Branches: Legislative

concepts.l: Structure of Congress: House vs. Senate
concepts.intro: The bicameral Congress splits legislative power between two chambers with different sizes, terms, and constitutional roles.
b: House of Representatives: 435 members, 2-year terms, apportioned by state population, more centralized leadership, rules limit floor debate (Rules Committee controls the agenda)
Senate: 100 members (2 per state), 6-year staggered terms (1/3 up for election every 2 years), allows unlimited debate (filibuster) unless cloture is invoked
The House has the sole power to initiate revenue (tax) bills and to impeach; the Senate has the sole power to try impeachments, confirm presidential appointments, and ratify treaties (2/3 vote)
Cloture requires 60 votes to end a filibuster and force a vote in the Senate — a key reason Senate action is slower and requires broader coalitions
Malapportionment concerns are addressed in the House via reapportionment after each decennial census and redistricting by state legislatures, which raises gerrymandering issues

concepts.l: How a Bill Becomes a Law
concepts.intro: Legislation must survive a multi-stage process with many potential veto points before becoming law.
b: A bill is introduced, referred to committee, where most bills die; committees hold hearings, markup sessions, and vote whether to report the bill out
In the House, the Rules Committee sets debate time and amendment rules; in the Senate, bills reach the floor by unanimous consent or after overcoming a filibuster via cloture
Both chambers must pass identical bill language; differences are resolved in a conference committee

The president can sign the bill into law, veto it (Congress can override with a 2/3 vote in both chambers), or take no action (bill becomes law after 10 days if Congress is in session, or is 'pocket vetoed' if Congress adjourns)

Committees are the real workhorses of Congress: standing committees (permanent, e.g., Ways and Means), select/special committees (temporary), joint committees (both chambers), and conference committees (reconcile differing bills)

concepts.intro: Article I, Section 8 grants Congress specific powers, supplemented by implied powers under the Necessary and Proper Clause.
b: Enumerated powers include the power to tax and spend, coin money, declare war, raise and support armies, and regulate interstate and foreign commerce
The 'power of the purse': Congress must appropriate all federal funds, giving it leverage over the executive branch and its programs
Oversight power: Congress monitors executive branch implementation of laws through hearings, investigations, and the confirmation process

Implied powers stem from the Necessary and Proper Clause, letting Congress act beyond a strict reading of enumerated powers (e.g., McCulloch v. Maryland upheld Congress's power to charter a national bank)

The commerce power has been interpreted broadly (Wickard v. Filburn expanded it to local, non-commercial activity affecting interstate commerce) but the Court has occasionally limited it (United States v. Lopez struck down the Gun-Free School Zones Act as exceeding the Commerce Clause)

concepts.l: Congressional Behavior: Representation and Trustee vs. Delegate
concepts.intro: Members of Congress must balance national policy goals against the demands of representing their home districts or states.
b: Delegate model: representatives vote according to the expressed wishes of their constituents, even against personal judgment
Trustee model: representatives use their own best judgment on behalf of constituents' broader interests
Politico model: representatives blend both approaches depending on the issue's salience and complexity
Descriptive representation means a representative shares constituents' demographic characteristics; substantive representation means acting in constituents' interests regardless of shared background
Incumbency advantage: incumbents win re-election at very high rates due to name recognition, franking privilege (free mail to constituents), casework, credit-claiming, and superior fundraising

concepts.intro: Party leaders and the committee system organize Congress's work and concentrate real legislative power outside the full floor vote.
b: The Speaker of the House, elected by the majority party, controls the floor agenda, committee assignments influence, and is second in the presidential line of succession
The Senate Majority Leader schedules floor business in the Senate but has less formal control than the Speaker due to Senate norms protecting individual senators' rights (e.g., filibuster, holds)
Committee chairs, typically the most senior majority-party member on a committee, wield major influence over which bills advance
Standing committees specialize by policy area (e.g., Armed Services, Judiciary) and are where most substantive bill-writing and vetting occurs
The conference committee reconciles differing House and Senate versions of a bill before a final vote in both chambers

concepts.intro: Every ten years, House seats are reapportioned among states and district lines are redrawn, a process with major political stakes.
b: Reapportionment: House seats (fixed at 435 total) are redistributed among states based on the decennial census population counts
Redistricting: state legislatures (in most states) redraw district boundaries within the state to reflect population shifts

Gerrymandering: drawing district lines to benefit a party or group — 'packing' concentrates opposition voters into few districts, 'cracking' spreads them thin across many districts to dilute their influence
Shaw v. Reno (1993): the Supreme Court ruled that redistricting based predominantly on race, absent a compelling justification, can violate the Equal Protection Clause
Because the Senate's apportionment (2 per state) is fixed by the Constitution, gerrymandering and reapportionment fights apply only to House districts

keyFacts: It takes 218 votes to pass a bill in the House (simple majority of 435) and typically 60 votes in the Senate to invoke cloture and end a filibuster
McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) established that Congress has implied powers under the Necessary and Proper Clause and that states cannot tax federal institutions
United States v. Lopez (1995) was the first case in decades to limit Congress's Commerce Clause power, striking down a law banning guns near schools
Divided government (different parties controlling the presidency and one or both chambers of Congress) tends to increase legislative gridlock
traps: The House has 435 voting members with 2-year terms; it is the Senate, not the House, that confirms appointments and ratifies treaties
A filibuster can be used only in the Senate, not the House, because House rules limit debate time
Reapportionment changes how many House seats each state gets; redistricting is the separate process of drawing the lines within a state — they are not the same thing
Implied powers come from the Necessary and Proper Clause, not from Article I's list of enumerated powers itself

quiz.q: According to John Locke's social contract theory, which natural rights precede government and must be protected by it?
o: Voting, jury trial, and due process
quiz.e: Locke identified life, liberty, and property as natural rights that government exists to secure, later echoed in the Declaration's 'life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.'

quiz.q: The United States is best classified as which form of government?
quiz.e: The U.S. is a republic in which citizens elect representatives to make laws, rather than voting directly on legislation.

quiz.q: Which weakness of the Articles of Confederation most directly caused Shays' Rebellion?
o: The national government could not tax or provide relief to indebted farmers
States could not trade with each other
quiz.e: Congress's lack of taxing power and inability to help economically distressed farmers left states unable to respond effectively, sparking the armed uprising.

quiz.q: The Great (Connecticut) Compromise resolved a dispute between the Virginia Plan and New Jersey Plan by creating:
o: A unicameral legislature based on population
A bicameral legislature with a population-based House and an equally-represented Senate
A judiciary with the power of judicial review
quiz.e: The compromise combined proportional representation (House) with equal state representation (Senate).

quiz.q: The Three-Fifths Compromise addressed which issue at the Constitutional Convention?
o: How to count enslaved people for representation and taxation
How many senators each state would have
How the president would be elected
quiz.e: It counted enslaved persons as three-fifths of a person when apportioning both representation and direct taxes.

quiz.q: In Federalist No. 10, Madison argues that the 'mischiefs of faction' are best controlled by:
o: An extended republic that dilutes any single faction's power
quiz.e: Madison argued a large republic with diverse interests prevents any one faction from dominating, since coalitions must span many competing groups.

quiz.q: Which power is an example of a power reserved to the states under the Tenth Amendment?
o: Establishing intrastate commerce regulations and local police powers
quiz.e: The Tenth Amendment reserves undelegated powers, such as general police power and local matters, to the states.

quiz.q: The Necessary and Proper Clause is significant because it:
o: Grants Congress implied powers to carry out its enumerated powers
Prohibits the federal government from taxing
quiz.e: Also called the Elastic Clause, it allows Congress to pass laws necessary to execute its Article I enumerated powers.

quiz.q: Which best distinguishes concurrent powers from enumerated powers?
o: Concurrent powers belong only to the states
Concurrent powers are shared by both national and state governments, while enumerated powers belong only to the national government
Enumerated powers are shared by both levels
quiz.e: Concurrent powers, like taxation, are exercised by both the federal government and the states; enumerated powers are listed specifically for the national government.

quiz.q: The Supremacy Clause (Article VI) establishes that:
o: Federal law and the Constitution take precedence over conflicting state laws
quiz.e: The Supremacy Clause makes the Constitution, federal laws, and treaties 'the supreme law of the land.'

quiz.q: Anti-Federalists like the author of Brutus No. 1 primarily feared that the proposed Constitution would:
o: Make the national government too weak to function
Create a central government so powerful it would threaten liberty and state sovereignty
quiz.e: Brutus No. 1 argued that a republic as extensive as the proposed union could not protect liberty and would consolidate too much power nationally.

quiz.q: The primary condition Anti-Federalists demanded before supporting ratification was:
quiz.e: Anti-Federalists insisted on explicit protections for individual liberties, leading to the first ten amendments in 1791.

quiz.q: In Federalist No. 51, Madison argues that liberty is protected chiefly by:
o: Dividing power among branches so 'ambition counteracts ambition'
quiz.e: Madison contended that separating power and giving each branch means to resist the others prevents any one branch from dominating.

quiz.q: Which scenario best illustrates a check on the legislative branch by the executive?
o: The Senate confirms a Cabinet nominee
The president vetoes a bill passed by Congress
The Supreme Court strikes down a law
quiz.e: A presidential veto directly checks Congress's lawmaking power; Congress can respond with a two-thirds override vote in both chambers.

quiz.q: Impeachment of a federal official requires:
o: A majority vote in the House to impeach, followed by a two-thirds Senate vote to convict
A two-thirds vote in the House only
quiz.e: The House impeaches by majority vote; conviction and removal require a two-thirds vote in the Senate.

quiz.q: Judicial review, the power of courts to declare laws unconstitutional, checks which branch(es)?
o: Both the legislative and executive branches
quiz.e: Judicial review allows courts to invalidate unconstitutional acts of both Congress and the president.

quiz.q: A key difference between the Virginia Plan and the New Jersey Plan was:
o: The Virginia Plan favored a unicameral legislature
The New Jersey Plan favored representation based on population
The Virginia Plan favored representation by population, while the New Jersey Plan favored equal representation per state
Both plans were identical on representation
quiz.e: Large states favored the Virginia Plan's population-based representation; small states favored the New Jersey Plan's equal representation.

quiz.q: Which amendment process describes how most constitutional amendments have actually been adopted?
o: Proposal by 2/3 of both houses of Congress, ratification by 3/4 of state legislatures
Proposal by a national convention, ratification by popular referendum
Proposal by the president, ratification by the Supreme Court
Proposal by 3/4 of states, ratification by Congress
quiz.e: All 27 amendments were proposed by two-thirds of both congressional chambers; all but one (the 21st) were ratified by state legislatures.

quiz.q: Cooperative federalism, often called 'marble cake' federalism, is best characterized by:
o: Strict separation of national and state functions
Overlapping and blended responsibilities between national and state governments, often through grants
States having no relationship with the federal government
quiz.e: Cooperative federalism blends federal and state roles, frequently using federal grants-in-aid to influence state policy.

quiz.q: A categorical grant differs from a block grant in that a categorical grant:
o: Comes with no restrictions on use
Is given for a specific, narrowly defined purpose with strings attached
Is only given to the executive branch
quiz.e: Categorical grants restrict funds to specific purposes, while block grants give states broader discretion over use.

quiz.q: The expansion of suffrage in the U.S. is illustrated by which sequence of constitutional amendments?
quiz.e: In chronological order, the 15th (1870) banned racial voting discrimination, 19th (1920) enfranchised women, 24th (1964) banned poll taxes, and 26th (1971) lowered the voting age to 18.

quiz.q: Pluralist theory of democracy holds that political power is:
o: Distributed among competing interest groups that bargain over policy
quiz.e: Pluralism sees policy as the outcome of competition and bargaining among many organized groups.

quiz.q: Elite theory of democracy contrasts with pluralism by arguing that:
o: A small number of wealthy or well-connected actors dominate policymaking
quiz.e: Elite theory holds that policy outcomes primarily reflect the preferences of a small, powerful elite rather than broad group competition.

quiz.q: Why did the Framers create the Electoral College instead of direct popular election of the president?
o: To guarantee the most populous state always wins
As a compromise between election by Congress and direct popular vote, also balancing large and small state influence
To eliminate the need for elections
To ensure the House chose the president
quiz.e: The Electoral College compromise gave states a role reflecting both population (House-based electors) and equal status (Senate-based electors).

quiz.q: Which of these is a power delegated exclusively to the national government?
quiz.e: Interstate commerce regulation is an enumerated power of Congress under Article I, Section 8.

quiz.q: Dual federalism, or 'layer cake' federalism, describes an era in which:
o: National and state governments' responsibilities were sharply separated and distinct
Federal and state powers were completely merged
The federal government controlled all local police forces
quiz.e: Dual federalism (roughly 1789–1930s) envisioned clearly separated spheres of authority for national and state governments.

quiz.q: The Bill of Rights was added to the Constitution primarily to:
o: Address Anti-Federalist concerns about protecting individual liberties from a strong national government
quiz.e: The first ten amendments responded directly to Anti-Federalist demands for explicit rights protections.

quiz.q: Which best describes the relationship between the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution?
o: The Declaration is legally binding law; the Constitution is not
The Declaration articulates founding principles like natural rights and consent of the governed; the Constitution establishes the structure of government
They were written by the same small group with identical purposes
quiz.e: The Declaration (1776) is a philosophical justification for independence; the Constitution (1787) is the actual framework of government.

quiz.q: A state passes a law directly conflicting with a valid federal statute. Under the Supremacy Clause, which prevails?
o: The state law, because states have reserved powers
Neither; the courts must write a new law
quiz.e: The Supremacy Clause makes valid federal law supreme over conflicting state law.

quiz.q: Which statement about the ratification debate is accurate?
o: Federalists supported ratification and a strong national government; Anti-Federalists opposed it, fearing centralized power
Both sides agreed a Bill of Rights was unnecessary
quiz.e: Federalists backed the Constitution and strong national government, while Anti-Federalists worried it endangered liberty and state authority.

quiz.q: The 'elastic' quality of the Necessary and Proper Clause refers to its:
o: Ability to expand congressional power to fit unforeseen circumstances
Fixed and unchangeable list of powers
quiz.e: Because it grants implied powers, the clause has been interpreted broadly ('elastically') to expand congressional authority over time, as in McCulloch v. Maryland.

quiz.q: Which situation best exemplifies a check by the judicial branch on the legislative branch?
o: The Supreme Court declares an act of Congress unconstitutional
The House votes on a budget
quiz.e: Judicial review lets the Supreme Court invalidate unconstitutional congressional statutes.

quiz.q: Why is the Constitution considered difficult to formally amend?
o: It requires only a simple majority in Congress
It requires supermajorities at both the proposal and ratification stages
Amendments can be made by executive order
States have no role in the process
quiz.e: The high bar of 2/3 congressional proposal and 3/4 state ratification (or convention alternatives) makes formal amendment rare.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of an implied power exercised by Congress?
quiz.e: Establishing a national bank is not explicitly listed in Article I but was upheld as an implied power under the Necessary and Proper Clause in McCulloch v. Maryland.

quiz.q: The framers' fear of concentrated power, informed by British rule, most directly led to which structural choice?
o: A single unified branch of government
Separation of powers and checks and balances across three branches
quiz.e: Distrust of unchecked authority led the Framers to divide national power among three branches with mutual checks.

quiz.q: Compared to the Articles of Confederation, the Constitution strengthened the national government by:
o: Creating an independent executive and judiciary and granting Congress taxing and commerce powers
Requiring unanimous consent for all laws
quiz.e: The Constitution fixed the Articles' key weaknesses by adding executive and judicial branches and granting Congress real taxing and commerce authority.

quiz.q: A grant-in-aid given to states with few restrictions, allowing broad discretion in spending within a general policy area, is called a:
quiz.e: Block grants provide funding for broad purposes (e.g., health, education) with fewer federal strings than categorical grants.

quiz.q: An unfunded mandate is best defined as:
o: A federal requirement imposed on states without accompanying federal funding to comply
A grant states can spend however they choose
A state law binding on the federal government
quiz.e: Unfunded mandates require state or local compliance with federal rules but do not provide the money to implement them, straining state budgets.

quiz.q: Federalist No. 10 and Brutus No. 1 disagree most fundamentally over:
o: Whether the president should be elected
Whether a large, extended republic can protect liberty and control factions
quiz.e: Madison (Fed. 10) argues an extended republic best controls factions; Brutus No. 1 argues a republic that large cannot preserve liberty or represent the people faithfully.

quiz.q: Which best explains why the Framers created a bicameral Congress?
o: To slow down lawmaking and balance large- and small-state interests via the Great Compromise
To ensure only the House could pass laws
To give the president control over both chambers
To eliminate the need for a Senate
quiz.e: Bicameralism, born of the Great Compromise, balances proportional (House) and equal (Senate) representation while adding a check within the legislature itself.

quiz.q: Which chamber of Congress has the sole constitutional power to ratify treaties?
o: Neither; treaties are ratified by the president alone
quiz.e: The Senate alone ratifies treaties, requiring a two-thirds vote.

quiz.q: A filibuster is a procedural tool available in which chamber?
quiz.e: The Senate's tradition of unlimited debate allows filibusters; the House limits debate time, making filibusters impossible there.

quiz.q: How many votes are needed to invoke cloture and end a Senate filibuster?
quiz.e: Cloture requires 60 votes under current Senate rules, a supermajority threshold.

quiz.q: Revenue (tax) bills must originate in which chamber of Congress?
quiz.e: The Constitution requires that all revenue bills originate in the House of Representatives.

quiz.q: Which body has the sole power to try impeachments?
quiz.e: The House impeaches (charges) an official; the Senate holds the trial and votes to convict by a two-thirds majority.

quiz.q: Most bills introduced in Congress die at which stage?
quiz.e: The vast majority of bills never make it out of committee, where they receive hearings and markup.

quiz.q: When the House and Senate pass different versions of the same bill, differences are resolved by a:
o: Second full floor vote in both chambers on a new bill
quiz.e: A conference committee, with members from both chambers, negotiates a single compromise version.

quiz.q: If the president neither signs nor vetoes a bill and Congress remains in session, what happens after 10 days?
o: The bill becomes law without the president's signature
The bill requires a new vote
quiz.e: A bill becomes law after 10 days (excluding Sundays) if Congress is in session and the president takes no action.

quiz.q: A 'pocket veto' occurs when:
o: The president signs a bill quietly
Congress adjourns within 10 days of sending a bill to the president, who takes no action, killing the bill
The Senate refuses to schedule a vote
quiz.e: If Congress adjourns before the 10-day period expires and the president has not signed, the bill dies without a formal veto.

quiz.q: Overriding a presidential veto requires:
o: A simple majority vote in both chambers
A two-thirds vote in both the House and Senate
quiz.e: Congress can override a veto only with a two-thirds supermajority in both chambers.

quiz.q: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) is significant because the Court ruled that:
o: Congress has implied powers under the Necessary and Proper Clause and states cannot tax federal institutions
The Commerce Clause has no limits
quiz.e: McCulloch upheld Congress's implied power to create a national bank and established federal supremacy over conflicting state action.

quiz.q: United States v. Lopez (1995) is significant because the Court:
o: Expanded the Commerce Clause without limit
Struck down a federal law as exceeding Congress's Commerce Clause power for the first time in decades
quiz.e: Lopez struck down the Gun-Free School Zones Act, holding that possessing a gun near a school was not sufficiently related to interstate commerce.

quiz.q: A member of Congress who votes strictly according to the expressed wishes of constituents, even against personal judgment, is acting as a:
quiz.e: The delegate model has representatives follow constituents' stated preferences directly.

quiz.q: A member of Congress who votes based on personal judgment about the constituents' best interests, even if it differs from expressed constituent opinion, is acting as a:
quiz.e: The trustee model has representatives exercise independent judgment on behalf of constituents.

quiz.q: Descriptive representation refers to:
o: Sharing constituents' demographic characteristics, such as race, gender, or background
quiz.e: Descriptive representation is about resembling one's constituents demographically, distinct from substantive (policy-based) representation.

quiz.q: Which factor contributes MOST to the incumbency advantage in congressional elections?
o: Name recognition, franking privilege, casework, and superior fundraising
quiz.e: Incumbents benefit from visibility, constituent services, free mail privileges, and easier fundraising, producing very high re-election rates.

quiz.q: The Speaker of the House is:
o: Elected by the full House and typically comes from the majority party
The most senior member regardless of party
quiz.e: The Speaker is elected by House members and is virtually always the majority party's leader.

quiz.q: Compared to the Speaker of the House, the Senate Majority Leader generally has:
o: More centralized control over the floor agenda
Less formal control, due to Senate norms protecting individual senators' rights like the filibuster
quiz.e: Senate rules and traditions, including unlimited debate, limit how much control any single leader can exert compared to the Speaker's power in the House.

quiz.q: Standing committees in Congress are best described as:
o: Permanent committees organized around specific policy areas
Committees composed of both chambers only
Committees that only exist during conference
quiz.e: Standing committees, like Ways and Means or Armed Services, are permanent and handle ongoing legislative work in their policy area.

quiz.q: Reapportionment refers to the process of:
o: Redrawing district lines within a state
Redistributing the 435 House seats among states based on the census
quiz.e: Reapportionment reallocates the fixed 435 House seats among states following the decennial census.

quiz.q: Redistricting refers to the process of:
o: Drawing new district boundaries within a state after reapportionment or population shifts
quiz.e: Redistricting is the drawing of specific district lines, usually done by state legislatures.

quiz.q: 'Packing' as a gerrymandering technique involves:
o: Spreading opposition voters thinly across many districts
Concentrating opposition voters into a small number of districts to waste their votes
quiz.e: Packing crams opposition supporters into few districts, reducing their influence elsewhere, while 'cracking' spreads them thin to dilute their power.

quiz.q: In Shaw v. Reno (1993), the Supreme Court ruled that:
o: Race can never be considered in redistricting
Redistricting drawn predominantly based on race, without compelling justification, can violate the Equal Protection Clause
quiz.e: Shaw v. Reno held that bizarre, race-based district shapes lacking sufficient justification could violate equal protection.

quiz.q: The 'power of the purse' refers to Congress's constitutional authority to:
o: Appropriate federal funds, giving it leverage over executive branch programs
quiz.e: Because federal spending requires congressional appropriation, Congress can use funding decisions to shape or restrain executive action.

quiz.q: Congressional oversight of the executive branch is exercised primarily through:
o: Direct control of agency budgets by the president alone
Committee hearings, investigations, and the confirmation process
quiz.e: Oversight lets Congress monitor and check how laws are being implemented, largely through committee hearings and investigations.

quiz.q: Which is an example of Congress exercising an implied, rather than enumerated, power?
o: Creating a national bank under the Necessary and Proper Clause
quiz.e: Chartering a national bank is not explicitly listed in Article I but was upheld as implied by the Necessary and Proper Clause in McCulloch v. Maryland.

quiz.q: Wickard v. Filburn (1942) expanded the Commerce Clause by ruling that:
o: Congress cannot regulate any local activity
Even wheat grown for personal, non-commercial use can be regulated because it affects interstate commerce in the aggregate
Only interstate sales can be regulated
Agriculture is exempt from federal regulation
quiz.e: Wickard held that local, non-commercial activity could still be regulated if it substantially affected interstate commerce when aggregated nationally.

quiz.q: Divided government occurs when:
o: One party controls both the presidency and all of Congress
Different parties control the presidency and at least one chamber of Congress
There is a tie in the Senate
quiz.e: Divided government, common in the modern era, often increases legislative gridlock as branches controlled by opposing parties struggle to compromise.

quiz.q: The House Rules Committee's primary function is to:
o: Set the terms of debate and amendment process for bills reaching the House floor
quiz.e: The Rules Committee, controlled by the majority party, determines how much debate and how many amendments a bill will get on the House floor.

quiz.q: Senators serve staggered six-year terms so that:
o: All senators are replaced at once
Roughly one-third of the Senate is up for election every two years, ensuring continuity
quiz.e: Staggered terms mean only about a third of Senate seats are contested in any election cycle, providing institutional continuity.

quiz.q: Which best explains why the Senate is often described as less responsive to short-term public opinion than the House?
o: Senators serve 2-year terms like House members
Senators serve longer, staggered 6-year terms representing entire states rather than smaller districts
quiz.e: Longer terms and statewide constituencies were designed to insulate senators somewhat from immediate shifts in public opinion.

quiz.q: A 'hold' in the Senate is a practice by which:
o: A senator formally blocks or delays a vote on a bill or nomination
The House delays sending a bill to the president
quiz.e: An individual senator can place a hold to delay floor action on a bill or nomination, reflecting the chamber's norm of protecting individual senators' leverage.

quiz.q: Casework performed by members of Congress refers to:
o: Helping individual constituents resolve problems with federal agencies
quiz.e: Casework is direct constituent service, helping individuals navigate federal bureaucracy — a major driver of incumbency advantage.

quiz.q: Why does the Senate confirmation process serve as a check on presidential power?
o: The Senate must approve major appointments (Cabinet, judges) and treaties before they take effect
quiz.e: Requiring Senate confirmation of key appointments and treaty ratification limits unilateral presidential action.

quiz.q: Which is true of the House compared to the Senate?
o: The House has more centralized leadership and stricter limits on debate
The House alone confirms judicial nominees
quiz.e: The House's larger size (435 members) requires more centralized control via leadership and the Rules Committee, unlike the Senate's tradition of open debate.

quiz.q: A committee chair's influence over legislation stems mainly from their power to:
o: Control the committee's agenda, including which bills receive hearings and votes
quiz.e: Chairs decide which bills get serious committee attention, effectively gatekeeping much of the legislative process.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an enumerated congressional power listed in Article I, Section 8?
quiz.e: Declaring war is explicitly enumerated in Article I, Section 8, distinguishing it from the president's implied commander-in-chief role in directing forces.

quiz.q: Why might a divided Congress (different parties controlling the House and Senate) struggle to pass major legislation?
o: Both chambers must pass identical bills, and differing majorities have differing priorities and procedural rules
One chamber must always defer to the other
The president automatically vetoes any such bill
quiz.e: Because both chambers must agree on identical legislation, opposing party control of each chamber makes compromise far harder.

quiz.q: A joint committee in Congress is composed of:
o: Members from both the House and Senate working on an ongoing basis (unlike a temporary conference committee)
quiz.e: Joint committees include members of both chambers and typically address ongoing matters like the economy or the Library of Congress, distinct from temporary conference committees.
